title: Brushed embroidery royal icing
subtitle: a piped and brushed technique that mimics fabric embroidery on a cake surface
excerpt: Brushed embroidery is a royal icing technique for decorating the surface of fondant-covered cakes. Wet icing is piped in the outline of a petal or leaf, then a damp brush draws through it to create a soft, feathered texture that looks like embroidery stitches. The technique works best on a firm, dry fondant surface.
sourceNotes: Brushed embroidery on cake became widespread in British sugarcraft from the 1970s onward, developed from traditional flat-icing decoration styles. The technique is taught in City and Guilds sugarcraft qualifications.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff white icing made from icing sugar and egg white or meringue powder. It dries hard and is used for piping and flooding decoration on cakes and biscuits.

content.text: Brushed embroidery is a way of painting textured floral or leaf patterns onto the surface of a fondant-covered cake using

. Wet icing is piped in a petal outline, then a damp brush draws inward across it to pull the icing into a feathered texture that looks like embroidery stitches. Work one petal at a time so the icing does not dry before you brush it.
The cake surface must be dry and firm. Leave a freshly covered cake at least 8 hours before painting.

Make a stiff royal icing with icing sugar and meringue powder or egg white. It should hold a peak without collapsing. Add a tiny amount of water until it flows smoothly off the tip without dripping. Colour as needed.
Transfer to a piping bag fitted with a small round tip (size 1 or 2). Lightly mark the design onto the cake surface with a pin or food-safe scriber.
Pipe the outline of one petal. Immediately dampen a fine brush (moist, not dripping) and draw from the outer edge inward to the centre. The icing should stretch into soft, brush-like marks.
Repeat petal by petal, cleaning the brush frequently. For layered flowers, let the lower petals dry for 5 minutes before piping the upper layer on top.
Add leaves and stems in the same way. A wider brush stroke and a slightly thinner icing gives a broader, more natural leaf texture. Allow the completed design to dry fully before moving the cake.

attrs.problem: Icing dries before you can brush it
attrs.avoid: Avoid doing more than one petal at a time; the icing surface skins within 30 seconds.
attrs.fix: Pipe one petal only, brush it immediately, then move to the next. Work away from draughts or direct heat.

attrs.problem: Brush marks tear the surface instead of feathering it
attrs.avoid: Avoid a dry brush or too much pressure; it will drag rather than pull.
attrs.fix: The brush should be barely damp. Too dry and it tears; too wet and the icing loses all texture. Blot the brush on a cloth before each stroke.

attrs.problem: Icing sinks into the fondant instead of sitting on top
attrs.avoid: Avoid working on fresh or soft fondant; it absorbs wet icing before it can hold its shape.
attrs.fix: Leave the covered cake overnight to form a firm skin before brushwork.
